passages.happening:
In the third year of King Belshazzar, Daniel has another vision (verse 1). In it he is in the citadel of Susa, in the province of Elam, beside the Ulai Canal (verse 2).

He sees a ram with two long horns, one longer than the other, the longer one growing up later (verse 3). The ram charges west, north and south. No animal can stand against him. ‘He did as he pleased and became great’ (verse 4).

Then a goat with a prominent horn between his eyes comes out of the west, ‘crossing the surface of the entire earth without touching the ground’ (verse 5). He rushes at the ram in a rage, shatters both its horns, throws it to the ground and tramples it (verses 6-7).

‘Thus the goat became very great, but at the height of his power, his large horn was broken off, and four prominent horns came up in its place, pointing toward the four winds of heaven’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
With this chapter the book returns to Hebrew and narrows its focus. Chapter 7 surveyed four kingdoms and the end of history. Chapter 8 looks closely at the second and third, Persia and Greece, and at one king who will rise from the Greek world.

The vision is dated to Belshazzar's third year, probably in the early 540s BC, while Babylon still stood. Susa, the capital of the old kingdom of Elam east of Babylon, would become one of the royal capitals of Persia. Daniel is there in the vision, not necessarily in body.

Here, unusually, the book names its own symbols (verses 20-21), and interpreters of every school agree on most of them. The ram's two horns are Media and Persia, the longer and later one Persia, which under Cyrus came to dominate the Medes and pushed west, north and south. The goat is Greece, and its great horn is Alexander the Great. He crossed from Europe in 334 BC and defeated the Persian Empire so fast it was as if he did not touch the ground. He died in Babylon in 323 BC at the height of his power, and his empire was divided among his generals into four main kingdoms.

Rams and goats were natural symbols for leaders, since they lead flocks, and horns stood for power throughout the Old Testament. The verb to become great runs through the vision, tracing the rise of each power.
passages.later: Susa appears again in the Bible as a Persian capital: ‘King Xerxes sat on his royal throne in the citadel of Susa’ (Esther 1:2), and Nehemiah was serving there ‘in the citadel of Susa’ (Nehemiah 1:1) when he heard of Jerusalem's ruined walls.
passages.asks: The ram did as he pleased and became great, until something greater came. Ask what in your own life is doing as it pleases and growing great. And ask what it would mean to hold power knowing that every horn in this vision is broken in the end.

passages.t: The little horn, and How long?
passages.happening:
From one of the four horns a little horn comes up. It grows toward the south and the east ‘and toward the Beautiful Land’ (verse 9). It grows as high as the host of heaven and throws some of the host and some of the stars to the earth and tramples them (verse 10).

‘It magnified itself, even to the Prince of the host; it removed His daily sacrifice and overthrew the place of His sanctuary’ (verse 11). The host and the daily sacrifice are given over to it, ‘and it flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did’ (verse 12).

Then Daniel hears two holy ones speaking. One asks, ‘How long until the fulfillment of the vision of the daily sacrifice, the rebellion that causes desolation, and the surrender of the sanctuary and of the host to be trampled?’ (verse 13). The answer: ‘It will take 2,300 evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be properly restored’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The Beautiful Land is Judea. The little horn that grows toward the south, the east and the Beautiful Land is widely identified as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 to 164 BC), the Seleucid king who campaigned in Egypt and the east, stopped the temple sacrifices in 167 BC and set up pagan worship in the sanctuary, until Judas Maccabeus rededicated it in December 164 BC. Some interpreters also see him as a pattern of a final opponent of God.

The daily sacrifice was the burnt offering presented every morning and evening at the temple, the heartbeat of Israel's worship. To stop it was to silence the covenant at its center. The host of heaven and the stars can refer to angels or stars, and here probably to God's people, whose struggle on earth is mirrored in heaven.

Antiochus took the title Epiphanes, meaning god made manifest. The Greek historian Polybius reports that some mocked him as Epimanes, the madman. The chapter's picture of a king who magnifies himself even to the Prince of the host captures a ruler who made himself the equal of God.

The question How long is the cry of the persecuted all through Scripture. The answer sets a limit to the desolation.
passages.later: The same cry rises in the Psalms: ‘How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?’ (Psalm 13:1). Zechariah hears an angel ask, ‘How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy from Jerusalem’ (Zechariah 1:12). And in Revelation the martyrs cry, ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood’ (Revelation 6:10).
passages.hard:
What do the 2,300 evenings and mornings mean?

The phrase can be read two ways. Many take it as 2,300 evening and morning sacrifices, that is, 1,150 days, a little over three years. Others take it as 2,300 full days, about six years and four months. Those who connect the vision with Antiochus IV note that the altar was desecrated in December 167 BC and rededicated in December 164 BC, three years later, and see the 1,150 days as close to that period, perhaps counted from an earlier event. Those who take 2,300 days look for a starting point in the troubles several years before the desecration.

In the nineteenth century some interpreters who read prophetic days as years used this verse to calculate Christ's return, most famously William Miller, whose prediction for 1844 was not fulfilled. Most interpreters today, conservative and critical alike, read the number as marking a limited period, set by God, for the desolation of the sanctuary. These notes calculate no date from it.
passages.asks: The holy ones ask How long, and the answer is a number with an end. Ask what you are asking God how long about. And ask whether you can trust that the trouble you are in has a limit you cannot yet see.

passages.t: Gabriel explains: Media and Persia, and Greece
passages.happening:
While Daniel tries to understand, someone with the appearance of a man stands before him (verse 15). A man's voice calls from the banks of the Ulai, ‘Gabriel, explain the vision to this man’ (verse 16).

As Gabriel comes near, Daniel is terrified and falls on his face. Gabriel calls him son of man and says, ‘understand that the vision concerns the time of the end’ (verse 17). Daniel falls into a deep sleep with his face to the ground, and Gabriel touches him and helps him up (verse 18).

Then Gabriel explains. ‘The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia’ (verse 20). ‘The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king’ (verse 21). The four horns are four kingdoms that will rise from that nation, but without the same power (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
This is the first time in the Bible an angel is named. Gabriel's name speaks of God's strength, or of a mighty man of God. He calls Daniel son of man, an ordinary term for a mortal, as God addresses Ezekiel. Here the phrase is not a title. It reminds Daniel that he is human, standing before a messenger from heaven.

The time of the end, in this chapter, is the end of the period of wrath the vision describes, the appointed time when the desolation will be over. Readers differ on how far beyond that the phrase reaches.

The interpretation names the first two powers outright, and readers of every school agree: Media and Persia, then Greece and its first great king, Alexander. The four horns are the kingdoms into which his empire was divided after his death, among them the Seleucids in Syria and the Ptolemies in Egypt, the two who would fight over Judea.
passages.later: The same angel appears in the Gospel of Luke: ‘I am Gabriel,’ he tells Zechariah, ‘I stand in the presence of God’ (Luke 1:19). And God calls Ezekiel by the same ordinary name: ‘Son of man,’ he says, ‘stand up on your feet’ (Ezekiel 2:1).
passages.asks: Daniel fell on his face, and the messenger touched him and stood him up. Ask whether you expect God's word to lift you or only to flatten you. And ask what it means to be called a mortal and still be spoken to by heaven.

passages.t: An insolent king, broken without human hands
passages.happening:
At the end of those kingdoms, ‘when the rebellion has reached its full measure, an insolent king, skilled in intrigue, will come to the throne’ (verse 23). ‘His power will be great, but it will not be his own’ (verse 24). He will cause terrible destruction, succeed in whatever he does, and destroy the mighty and the holy people.

By craft he will make deceit prosper. ‘In his own mind he will make himself great’ (verse 25). In a time of peace he will destroy many, and he will even stand against the Prince of princes. ‘Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands’ (verse 25).

Gabriel says the vision is true, and tells Daniel to seal it up, ‘for it concerns the distant future’ (verse 26). ‘I, Daniel, was exhausted and lay ill for days’ (verse 27). Then he gets up and goes about the king's business, confounded by what he has seen.
passages.hearers:
Readers on all sides most often identify this king with Antiochus IV, who came to the throne by intrigue, made himself great, attacked the holy people and stood against God. His power was not his own: the book insists that every king rules by God's leave. And he is broken off not by human hands, as the stone in chapter 2 was cut out not by human hands. His end comes from God.

The Prince of princes is God himself. The king's sin is the same as Belshazzar's and Nebuchadnezzar's before his humbling: he makes himself great in his own mind, and sets himself against heaven.

The chapter closes with Daniel ill and confounded. And then he goes back to work. He gets up and does the king's business. The first hearers were shown a man who carried a terrible vision and still did his ordinary duty the next day.
passages.later: Chapter 11 traces the same king's career in detail: ‘a despicable person will arise; royal honors will not be given to him, but he will come in a time of peace and seize the kingdom by intrigue’ (Daniel 11:21). And the stone of the king's dream was likewise ‘cut out, but not by human hands’ (Daniel 2:34). A psalm pictures God laughing at the plots of proud kings: ‘The One enthroned in heaven laughs’ (Psalm 2:4).
passages.asks: Daniel was overwhelmed by what he saw, and then he went about the king's business. Ask how you carry hard knowledge and still do your ordinary work. And ask what it means for your fears that the power of every insolent ruler ‘will not be his own’ (verse 24).
